info.bio: Elizabeth Clark "Liz" Phair es una cantautora y guitarrista norteamericana. Su carrera musical comenzó a principios de los 90 y fue una de las principales artistas del movimiento independiente DIY de la década; enfocado más que todo al sonido lo-fi; sin embargo, desde el lanzamiento de su cuarto álbum, Phair ha optado por un sonido más pulido y trabajado en estudio. Su más reciente álbum, "Somebody's Miracle" marcó el final de su contrato con Captiol Records; la artista firmó con ATO Records a principios del 2008

scenes.name: Cantautoras de los noventa
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Las mujeres tienen sus propios estilos, en plural: Azalia Snail y su psicodelia lo-fi, Jarboe, Lida Husik (entre la cantante pop y la pintora sonora), Robin Holcomb, Lisa Germano (Geek The Girl, «un viaje dantesco a la psique de una chica»), Tori Amos, Juliana Hatfield, Kristin Hersh, Jewel, Natalie Merchant, Cat Power (Moon Pix), Edith Frost, Lauryn Hill, Shannon Wright. Las «grrrls» más airadas: Lois Maffeo, Ani DiFranco, PJ Harvey (Dry, Rid Of Me), Liz Phair (Exile In Guyville), DQE, Aimee Mann, Sheryl Crow, Alanis Morissette, Neko Case. Y los paisajes sonoros de Björk, la cantautora más influyente de la década, Kate St John, Natacha Atlas, Heather Duby, Solex y Beth Orton.

podcast.title: Alt Rock Madonna Comparison
podcast.body: Liz Phair was often seen as the alt-rock counterpart to Madonna, embodying a defiant "Get out of my way" attitude coupled with a self-assured and challenging sexuality. "In many ways, Liz was the alt rock version of some of the characteristics Madonna had."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Artistic Comparison (1990s)
podcast.body: Liz Phair was mentioned as an artist, along with Alanis Morissette and Courtney Love, who could be "contained and marketed and categorized," in contrast to Sinead O'Connor, whose unique intensity prevented easy classification. "Unlike, say, Alanis Morissette, Liz Fair, Courtney Love, and a few others, Shanade could never be contained and marketed and categorized."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bedroom Recordings as Girly Sound (Early 1990s)
podcast.body: In Chicago, Liz Phair was part of the burgeoning low-fidelity scene by making cassettes of her songs in her bedroom under the name Girly Sound. This practice of recording in an intimate, home setting on basic equipment was a hallmark of the lo-fi movement, prioritizing raw artistic expression. "In Chicago, a woman named Liz Fair was making cassettes of her songs in her bedroom using the name Gurley Sound."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Current Work
podcast.body: Currently, Liz Phair composes music for television, notably for the program *The 100*. "These days, Liz works composing music for television. You know a program called The 100? That's all Liz's music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Empowerment for Women
podcast.body: Many women found Liz Phair's sexually frank attitude refreshing and empowering, admiring her willingness to be as open about sexuality as any man. "Many women found that attitude refreshing and empowering and it's something to be admired."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Feminist Attitude and Sexuality
podcast.body: Liz Phair emerged from Chicago with a strong feminist attitude, openly celebrating female sexuality in an uncompromisingly explicit way. She has documented her story in a couple of memoirs. "Liz Fair, strong feminist, came out of Chicago with an attitude that celebrated female sexuality in an uncompromisingly explicit way."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Driven By Her: Women Who Rocked The 90's

podcast.title: Influence from Galaxie 500
podcast.body: Liz Phair acknowledged Galaxie 500 as a significant influence on her own musical development, indicating the band's impact beyond their commercial success.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Projection of Strength and Sexuality
podcast.body: Liz Phair's appeal in 1994 stemmed from her confident projection of strength and an unashamed expression of sex and sexuality, which she viewed as a source of power. Her attitude challenged the conventional, often demure, portrayals of female performers from prior decades, presenting a modern, real, honest, and smart persona. "For her, sex and sexuality was a strength, something powerful, something that should be expressed with no shame and nothing to apologize for."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Blackie O'Nassis Death (June 13, 2023) – Drummer on Pulp Fiction's "Girl, You'll Be a Woman Soon"; Age 57, Cause Unknown
xref.body: John Rowan, who played under the name Blackie O'Nassis, was the drummer for Urge Overkill — the Chicago band whose cover of Neil Diamond's "Girl, You'll Be a Woman Soon" (1967) appears in the famous dance scene in *Pulp Fiction*. The band was also a cult favorite in the alt-rock community and opened for Nirvana on the *Nevermind* tour, during which they befriended Kurt Cobain, Chrissie Hynde of the Pretenders, and Liz Phair. Blackie left the band in 1996; there were reports of heroin use and at least one arrest. The cause of his death on June 13, 2023, at age 57 was never disclosed. "As for the cause of his death on June 13th, 2023, we have no idea."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Artistic Comparison (1990s)

"Unlike, say, Alanis Morissette, Liz Fair, Courtney Love, and a few others, Shanade could never be contained and marketed and categorized."

xref.title: Artistic Comparison (1990s)
xref.body: Courtney Love was mentioned as an artist, along with Alanis Morissette and Liz Phair, who could be "contained and marketed and categorized," in contrast to Sinead O'Connor, highlighting O'Connor's distinct and uncontainable artistic persona. "Unlike, say, Alanis Morissette, Liz Fair, Courtney Love, and a few others, Shanade could never be contained and marketed and categorized."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Comparison to Other Female Artists (1990s)
xref.body: Unlike artists such as Alanis Morissette, Liz Phair, and Courtney Love, Sinead O'Connor was viewed as too intense to be "contained and marketed and categorized." Her fierce independence and uncompromising nature set her apart, and her influence in the 1990s was widespread. "Unlike, say, Alanis Morissette, Liz Fair, Courtney Love, and a few others, Shanade could never be contained and marketed and categorized."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Other Artists
xref.body: Despite modest record sales, Galaxie 500 was cited by influential artists, including members of Sonic Youth and Liz Phair, as being very important to their own music.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
